G1037.detail: 1. The word designates the great marine depths, the abyss or the gulf beneath the surface of the ocean — something so deep and dark that one cannot see or reach the bottom. It is the concrete image of dark and fearsome waters. 2. In Paul's account in 2 Corinthians 11:25, "the abyss" refers to the experience of being one day and one night in the open sea, engulfed by the waves, in the anguish of possible death. The word thus evokes not only geographical depth but also the vertiginous and deadly trial of one who is thrown into these waters.
G1037.origine: The Greek word βυθός comes from a root that expresses the idea of depth and bottom. It regularly translates the Hebrew words מְצוּלָה (metsoulah) and מְצוֹלָה (metsolah) in the Greek Old Testament, which denote the marine depths. The family of the Greek word is limited, but the image is very ancient: since biblical times, the marine abyss symbolizes chaos, danger, and the inaccessible.
G1037.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament: in 2 Corinthians 11:25. Paul lists the perils he faced in the service of the Gospel, mentioning three shipwrecks. After his last shipwreck, he spent a day and a night "in the abyss" — that is, floating or swimming in the open sea. This passage gives the word its only direct usage in the New Testament, but it shows that βυθός retains its concrete and terrifying sense of marine depth where one finds oneself alone in the face of danger.
G1037.portee: This account of Paul shows that even the apostles faced extreme trials — shipwreck, imminent drowning — and had to call upon the power of God to survive. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that trust in Jesus does not immunize us against the storms of life, but that one who surrenders to God can traverse the most terrifying abysses.

sens: One who works with leather by cleaning, treating, and preparing it
Craftsman who transforms raw hides into usable leather
G1038.detail: 1. A tanner is a craftsman who prepares animal hides to make leather: he cleans, treats, and softens the raw hides. It is a manual job, practiced in a workshop, often near water (as indicated by Simon's house near the sea in Acts 10:6). 2. The profession of tanner was considered impure in Jewish culture, as working with animal carcasses was defiling according to the Law. It is significant that Peter, the apostle to the Jews, stays with Simon the tanner (Acts 9:43): this shows his gradual break with ritual purity prejudices, which prepares him for his vision in Acts 10 where he receives the divine command to eat formerly unclean foods.
G1038.origine: The Greek word comes from "byrsa" (hide, skin), from which also comes "byrsodépés" (an older form of the same profession). The word literally designates one who works with byrsa, the raw hide. It is a term from late Greek that shows how Greek adapted to name the artisanal trades of the Roman world.
G1038.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the same account in Acts: Peter stays with Simon the tanner in Joppa (Acts 9:43, 10:6, 10:32). This recurring geographical and social detail — the proximity to the sea — emphasizes Simon's concrete artisanal activity. It is in this house that Peter receives his transformative vision that prepares him to welcome the centurion Cornelius and to understand that the Gospel is also for the Gentiles.
G1038.portee: This humble word reveals how God uses simple encounters, everyday life, to accomplish His purposes. It is in a craftsman's house, with a man who practices a ritually despised trade, that the Holy Spirit prepares Peter's heart for a new understanding of divine will. This reminds us that God does not overlook our ordinary places of life and that He can speak to us anywhere.

sens: Very fine and precious linen fabric, of dazzling whiteness
Luxury garment worn by the rich and powerful
Festive and glorious adornment, worthy of the heavens
G1039.detail:
1. Fine linen is a fabric made from the fibers of the flax plant, woven with great care to become very fine, soft, and white. It is one of the most precious fabrics of antiquity, more luxurious than ordinary linen. In Babylon, this fabric ranks among the most valued goods, alongside gold and precious stones (Revelation 18:12).
2. In the biblical world, only the rich and powerful wore garments of fine linen. The great city of Babylon was clothed in it, as a sign of its extreme wealth and pride (Revelation 18:16), just like the kings and nobles of the earth.
3. The Bible uses fine linen to describe celestial splendor and righteousness. The Bride of the Lamb, that is, the Church, is clothed in fine white and pure linen which represents "the righteous deeds of the saints" (Revelation 19:8). The heavenly armies following Christ the King also wear this royal garment (Revelation 19:14), showing that fine linen is the adornment of divine glory and eternal holiness.
G1039.origine: The Greek word βύσσινος comes from βύσσος, which designates fine linen itself. In Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, this fabric is called שֵׁשׁ (shesh) or בּוּץ (bouz), and the Greek translation of the Hebrew text often uses βύσσος to translate it. It was a fabric of great value, imported from Egypt and the East, reserved for the elite and temples.
G1039.emploi: The word appears four times in Revelation, all in chapters 18 and 19, which describe the end of Babylon and the heavenly vision of the Lord. First, it designates a commercial good, a symbol of earthly wealth destined to perish (Revelation 18:12, 16). Then, it takes on a spiritual meaning: it describes the garment of the Bride of Christ, which is not material wealth but the visible expression of the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). Finally, it characterizes the heavenly army of the King of kings, manifesting the power and holiness of Christ (Revelation 19:14). The contrast is striking: the same fabric first symbolizes human pride destined for judgment, then the true and eternal glory of God.
G1039.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on true wealth. The Babylonian fine linen, however precious it may be, disappears in an hour. But the fine linen of the Bride of Christ — which costs nothing to acquire, as it consists of the righteous deeds of the saints — remains for eternity. By choosing to live in righteousness and holiness rather than pursuing the riches of the world, the Christian prepares to don this unchanging celestial adornment.

sens: Very fine and soft linen fabric of great quality
Luxury garment worn by the wealthy and high-ranking individuals
Symbol of wealth and material well-being
G1040.detail:
1. Fine linen is a precious fabric made from very fine and tightly woven flax fibers, producing a soft, shiny, and very expensive cloth. It was a luxury item in antiquity, difficult to obtain and very costly. In Luke 16:19, the rich man in the parable wears fine linen, immediately indicating his wealth: only an extremely prosperous man could afford to dress this way every day.
2. Fine linen represents a prestigious garment reserved for those in power and high status. It is a visible symbol of the material wealth and luxury accessible to someone, and by wearing fine linen, one publicly displays their privileged condition.
G1040.origine: The Greek word bussos (and its Hebrew equivalent bouz) refers to a textile plant from which the finest and most sought-after fibers of the ancient world are derived. The term comes from the East, as fine linen was primarily produced in Egypt, in the Nile Valley, where it was crafted with unparalleled skill. Ancient Greek translators rendered various Hebrew terms for linen and fine cloth with this Greek word.
G1040.emploi: The word bussos appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:19, in the parable of the rich man and poor Lazarus. Jesus mentions it to characterize the rich man right from the first sentence: this man was dressed in purple and fine linen, meaning the two most luxurious and prestigious fabrics known. This mention immediately establishes the contrast between this rich man living in excessive luxury and poor Lazarus lying at his gate. The use of fine linen emphasizes not only the character's material wealth but also his moral indifference to the suffering of others.
G1040.portee: This parable reminds the disciples that material wealth and sumptuous clothing do not constitute true life, and that accumulating luxury while ignoring the distress of the poor attracts divine judgment. The contrast between the rich man's fine linen and Lazarus's nakedness invites every believer to examine how they use their possessions: with generosity towards the needy or with selfish indifference.

sens: An elevated platform
A place of worship intended for offerings and sacrifices
Figuratively: an object or cause that is honored as sacred
G1041.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to an elevated platform or surface, meaning a structure made to dominate the space and be well visible.
2. But above all, it is an altar: a structure on which offerings are presented and worship is celebrated. It is the place where the deity is honored.
3. By extension, it also refers to what is revered, what is treated as sacred (Acts 17:23: Paul discovers in Athens an altar "To an unknown god," which shows how pagans dedicated places to powers they did not truly know).
G1041.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and designates a platform or elevated place (from βαίνω, "to go up"). In Hebrew, the terms מִזְבְּחַ (mizbeaḥ) or בָּמָה (bamah) were used to refer to the altar: it was a high place, visible from afar, where one turned to the divine.
G1041.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:23. Paul finds himself in Athens and observes the altars of the Greek gods. He even notices an altar dedicated "To an unknown god," which becomes for him an opportunity to proclaim the true God. This context shows how pagans used altars to honor deities, often without even knowing who they truly were.
G1041.portee: This passage reminds the reader that humanity instinctively seeks the divine, even when it is unaware of it. The altar "to an unknown god" in Athens symbolizes this confused spiritual thirst. For the Christian, this underscores the importance of proclaiming the truth of the living God to those who seek Him without knowing Him, and guiding hearts towards true worship.

sens: The stone pavement where Pilate rendered his judgment against Jesus
G1042.detail: 1. Gabbatha is the Aramaic name for a stone-paved platform located in Jerusalem, where the Roman governor Pilate held his tribunal. It is on this elevated place, also called "the Pavement" in Greek, that Pilate sat to pronounce his sentence of condemnation against Jesus (John 19:13). The word evokes both a public space, an official place of power, and the decisive moment when Jesus was judged and delivered to death.
G1042.origine: Gabbatha is an Aramaic word transliterated into Greek. The Gospel of John relates it to the Greek term "lithóstroton" (πάτος), which literally means "paving of stones." Although the exact Aramaic etymology remains uncertain, this proper name preserves the memory of a real place in Jerusalem, the paved floor of the Roman praetorium where imperial justice was exercised.
G1042.emploi: John is the only one to mention this place by its Aramaic name (John 19:13). The evangelist emphasizes that it is a named place, known to contemporary readers, and he immediately provides the Greek equivalent for his Greek-speaking readers. This topographical detail roots the event of the passion in a precise and verifiable geographical reality. Pilate sits there as the supreme judge, investing this pavement with Roman political power, before pronouncing the verdict that changes the course of history.
G1042.portee: This place holds considerable spiritual significance: it is where the drama of the cross unfolds, where the Son of God was unjustly judged by human power. Gabbatha symbolizes the moment when the world rejected Jesus, but also the passage to salvation. For the Christian, this stone pavement evokes the solidity of the gospel narrative and invites reflection on the price of redemption acquired at this cost.

sens: The archangel, that is, the superior messenger who stands in the presence of God
G1043.detail: 1. Gabriel is one of the most important celestial beings, an archangel tasked with delivering God's messages to humanity. His name means "hero of God" or "strength of God" in Hebrew. He stands directly before the throne of God (Luke 1:19), indicating his exceptional status among celestial beings. It is in this capacity that he is sent to fulfill the most solemn missions to humans.
G1043.origine: The name Gabriel comes from Hebrew *gabar* (to be strong, to be powerful) and *El* (God), which literally means "the strength of God" or "God is my strength." This name expresses both the divine power and authority that this angel carries. In the Greek Old Testament, Gabriel also appears in the book of Daniel to announce events of great prophetic importance.
G1043.emploi: Gabriel appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Luke at the beginning of his Gospel. First appearance: he presents himself to the priest Zechariah in the Temple to announce the imminent birth of John the Baptist, and he identifies himself as one who "stands before God" (Luke 1:19). Second appearance: six months later, God sends him to Nazareth to announce to Mary that she will give birth to the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:26). These two announcements mark the beginning of the narrative of the incarnation according to Luke.
G1043.portee: Gabriel embodies the certainty that God communicates with His people through His celestial messengers. His visits mark crucial moments in the plan of salvation: they introduce the coming of Jesus and call for faith despite disbelief or fear. For the reader, Gabriel reminds us that the sovereign God acts in human history and sends His messengers to prepare and announce His work.

sens: Disease of flesh that necroses and decays
Destructive propagation that gradually spreads
Figuratively: that which corrodes and spiritually destroys
G1044.detail:
1. Gangrene is a serious disease where flesh becomes mortified and rots, progressively affecting other parts of the body. It arises from infected or poorly treated wounds. In 2 Timothy 2:17, Paul uses it to describe how the ungodliness of certain individuals (Hymenaeus and Philetus) spreads: like gangrene that devours tissue, their corrupt words gradually "eat away" at the faith of the listeners and lead them away from the truth.
2. Figuratively, it refers to any corruption or bad influence that spreads uncontrollably, gradually contaminating the whole body. Paul chooses this medical image to illustrate the seriousness of spiritual danger: heresy does not remain isolated; it progresses and threatens the entire community, just as untreated gangrene destroys the whole body.
G1044.origine: The Greek word γάγγραινα comes from a root expressing the idea of gnawing or devouring. The term belongs to Greek medical vocabulary and literally means a wound that devours healthy flesh. It is a very concrete and tangible image that would have been familiar to ancient readers confronted with infectious diseases without antibiotics.
G1044.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:17. Paul uses it to warn against false teachings and ungodly words that, like gangrene, silently progress and gradually destroy the spiritual health of the church. It is a shocking figure, intended to alarm readers and motivate them to combat heresy from its beginnings, before it spreads.
G1044.portee: This image of gangrene challenges Christians about the danger of false teachings and doctrinal compromise. It reminds that spiritual corruption, like physical gangrene, does not stop on its own: it worsens and spreads. It calls for active vigilance: to discern errors, reject them quickly, and protect the Christian community from the poison of false doctrines before it spreads too far.

sens: son of Jacob and Leah
tribe of Israel descended from Gad
portion of the territory of Israel occupied by the tribe of Gad
G1045.detail:
1. Gad is one of the twelve sons of Jacob, born to his wife Leah (Genesis 30:11). His name means "good fortune" in Hebrew, celebrating divine providence at his birth.
2. From this son of Jacob comes the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. This tribe appears among the communities of God's people throughout biblical history, notably in the eschatological count of Revelation where twelve thousand members of the tribe of Gad are sealed with the divine seal (Revelation 7:5).
3. The tribe of Gad also receives as an inheritance a portion of territory east of the Jordan, a fertile region between the Jordan Valley and the desert.
G1045.origine: The name Gad comes from the Hebrew גָּד (Gad), which means "good fortune" or "luck." This term reflects Leah's joy at the birth of this son, expressed by the exclamation "What good fortune!" (Genesis 30:11). The Hebrew word has been retained without translation in the Greek text of the New Testament, as is customary for proper names of the tribes of Israel.
G1045.emploi: Gad appears in Revelation (7:5) in an eschatological vision where the twelve tribes of Israel are listed and marked with the divine seal at the end of times. This enumeration recalls the twelve tribes founded by the twelve sons of Jacob, including Gad. In this context, the mention of Gad emphasizes the integrity and completeness of God's saved people, each tribe having its share in eternal salvation.
G1045.portee: The tribe of Gad reminds that God works for the good ("good fortune") of His people. In the context of Revelation, the explicit inclusion of Gad among the sealed tribes affirms that none are forgotten in God's final salvation: each tribe, each part of the inherited people, will have its place in eternal redemption.

sens: inhabitants of Gadara, city of Perea
G1046.detail: 1. The Gadarenians are the inhabitants of Gadara, an important city located in Perea (a region east of the Jordan). The term designates the peoples who lived in this area.
G1046.origine: The Greek word Gadarēnos derives from the name of the city of Gadara, the capital of Perea. It is an adjective formed from the name of the city to indicate origin or belonging to this place. Gadara was a prosperous Hellenistic city in the territory of the Decapolis.
G1046.emploi: The term appears only once in the Gospel of Matthew (8:28), in the account of Jesus crossing the lake and arriving in the land of the Gadarenians. It is there that He encounters two men possessed by demons, who came out of the tombs. Other parallel accounts (Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26) use different textual variants ("Gergesenes"), but Matthew clearly identifies this territory as that of the Gadarenians.

sens: Collection of accumulated and stored wealth
Precious resources entrusted to the care of a responsible person
G1047.detail:
1. The word refers to a collection of riches, valuable objects, and money amassed and reserved. It is the image of an accumulation of precious goods kept carefully, like the gold or silver of a king. In Acts 8:27, the Ethiopian eunuch is "in charge of all his treasures," meaning he is responsible for all the wealth of Queen Candace.
2. The word can also refer to these riches from an administrative perspective: it is the total financial or material resources of a state or sovereign, entrusted to an officer who is in charge of them. The title "steward of the treasures" shows that it is an official function and a major responsibility with the royal power.
G1047.origine: The word γάζα comes from Persian and specifically refers to royal treasure. It is a borrowing from a foreign language, reflecting that the system of centralized treasury was particularly developed in Persian and Eastern empires. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words that denote deposits of royal wealth (such as "genzin" in biblical Aramaic).
G1047.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:27. It is found in the account of the conversion of the Ethiopian eunuch, where it serves to describe the rank and responsibility of this man: he is a high official of the kingdom of Ethiopia, tasked with administering royal wealth. Its use emphasizes the importance and authority of this character, who was a powerful and esteemed man in his country before his encounter with Philip.
G1047.portee: The mention of royal treasure highlights that the Gospel reaches all levels of society — including the powerful and the rich. This eunuch, despite his high position and wealth, feels the spiritual need to worship God and ultimately receives baptism. This shows that human wealth and power do not satisfy spiritual thirst, and that every person, regardless of social status, is called to seek God.

sens: City in the southwest of ancient Canaan, one of the five main cities of the Philistines.
G1048.detail: Gaza was a fortified city on the Mediterranean coast, a major center of Philistine territory in antiquity. It occupied a strategic position in Canaan, southwest of Judah. In the New Testament, it appears only once: in Acts 8:26, the Spirit directs Philip to take the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza, this desert road where he will meet the Ethiopian eunuch and preach Christ to him.
G1048.origine: The Hebrew name עַזָּה (azza) designated this Philistine city since antiquity. The city was known as a major trading hub due to its position on trade routes. In the Old Testament, it often embodies the power and resistance of the enemies of God's people.
G1048.emploi: Gaza is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:26. The context is the expansion of the Gospel after the martyrdom of Stephen: Philip, one of the seven deacons, receives the Spirit's command to go to the deserted road leading to Gaza. It is there that he will meet and convert the eunuch of the treasury of Candace, queen of Ethiopia. This journey symbolizes the advance of the Gospel to the ends of the known world.
G1048.portee: The mention of Gaza reminds us how the Gospel crosses geographical and cultural boundaries. Philip obeys the Spirit to follow a deserted path, showing that God guides His disciples to the souls He wants to save, even in unexpected and remote places.

sens: Chest or box in the temple where worshippers deposited their monetary offerings
Treasure or box of a temple, place where sacred funds were kept
G1049.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the chests with a trumpet-shaped opening, placed in the temple of Jerusalem, where worshippers threw their coins as offerings (Mark 12:41, Luke 21:1). Jesus sits opposite these chests to observe how each person gives: the rich put in much, but a poor widow gives little and receives His praise because she gives all she has.
2. The word can also refer to the temple treasury itself, the sacred place where the riches of worship were kept (John 8:20). It is near the treasury that Jesus teaches in the temple, in a safe place.
G1049.origine: The Greek word is formed from two roots: "gaz" (from Persian, meaning treasure or wealth) and "phylakè" (guard, protection). It literally means a "guarded place" for treasures. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew "lishkah" (chamber, cell) and "nishkah" (recess), which referred to the rooms in the temple where sacred offerings were stored.
G1049.emploi: The word appears four times in the Gospels, always referring to temple offerings. Mark and Luke translate it as "chest" when describing the episode where Jesus observes people giving (Mark 12:41, 43; Luke 21:1): it is a teaching moment where Jesus praises the poor and sincere gift above the abundant but vain gift. John uses it once to refer to the "treasury" of the temple, that is, the sanctuary where the sacred wealth rested, and this is in John 8:20, in a context of teaching and divine security.
G1049.portee: This word reminds us that in true worship, what matters is not the amount given, but the heart and sacrifice of the giver. The lesson from the temple chest invites Christians to examine their own offerings: do they give out of habit and calculation, or with sincerity and detachment? It is a word from Jesus about the real spiritual measure of our actions before God.

sens: Christian from Macedonia, traveling companion of Paul
Christian from Derbe
Christian from Corinth, host of Paul
Recipient of the third epistle of John
G1050G.detail:
1. Gaius of Macedonia is a disciple who accompanies Paul during his missionary journey. In Acts 19:29, during the riot in Ephesus caused by the silversmiths, he is arrested along with Aristarchus and dragged into the theater, showing his involvement in the apostolic work.
2. Another Gaius lives in the city of Derbe, in Asia Minor, and is among those who accompany Paul in his travels.
3. Gaius of Corinth is a prosperous Christian who welcomes Paul into his home and receives the entire church in his house, making him a generous community leader.
4. A Gaius is the direct recipient of the third epistle of John, where the apostle praises his hospitality and faithfulness to the truth.
G1050G.origine: Gaius is a common Latin name in the Roman world, borne by many personalities of the time. It has no particular biblical etymology, but its use in the New Testament reflects the integration of disciples into the Greco-Roman culture of the first century.
G1050G.emploi: The name Gaius appears four times in the New Testament, designating four distinct disciples. The most documented is the one from Corinth, who in Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14 is presented as a resourceful man, capable of hosting Paul and the entire community. The one from Macedonia, mentioned in Acts 19:29, illustrates how converts risked their safety to follow the Gospel. These characters embody the type of generous Christians who actively supported the apostolic mission.
G1050G.portee: The different Gaiuses testify to the diversity of disciples in the first century: itinerant travelers, welcoming hosts, men of substance who put their resources at the service of the Church. Their existence reminds us that behind the great names of the apostles, a multitude of ordinary believers built and supported the early Christian communities through their hospitality, faithfulness, and courage.

sens: Disciple from Macedonia mentioned in Acts
Disciple from Derbe who accompanied Paul
Disciple from Corinth to whom Paul wrote
Recipient of the third epistle of John
G1050H.detail: 1. Gaius was a common name in Greco-Roman antiquity, borne by several first-century Christians mentioned in the New Testament. 2. One of them was from Macedonia (Acts 19:29), a disciple in this region of northern Greece. 3. Another came from Derbe, a city in Phrygia, and traveled with the apostle Paul to accompany him to Asia (Acts 20:4), showing his commitment to support the apostolic ministry. 4. A third Gaius resided in Corinth: Paul personally baptized him and greets him as his friend in his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:23), indicating his importance in the local church. 5. Finally, a fourth Gaius received the third epistle of John, which shows us a pastor concerned with hospitality towards itinerant missionaries and faithfulness to the Christian truth.
G1050H.origine: Gaius (or Gaius in Latin) is a very common Roman name, without particular biblical etymology. The name simply evokes the identity of these men integrated into the life of the early Church and recognized by name by the apostles.
G1050H.emploi: The New Testament mentions at least four men named Gaius in the Christian communities. Acts 20:4 shows him as a traveling companion of Paul, suggesting that he was a committed and trustworthy disciple. Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14 designate a Gaius from Corinth, a local official or notable who offered hospitality to the apostles. The third epistle of John addresses a Gaius, probably an exemplary church leader in his charity. These mentions highlight the role of ordinary disciples in supporting the apostolic ministry.
G1050H.portee: These brief mentions of Gaius remind the reader that the life of the early Church relied on ordinary, faithful, and generous men and women, whose names are preserved by God. They encourage Christians to recognize that every act of hospitality, support for the service of the Gospel, and faithfulness to the truth has value in the eyes of the Lord, even if it never becomes famous.

sens: Christian from Corinth, friend and host of Paul
G1050I.detail: Gaius is a name borne by several characters in the New Testament. This one refers to the Christian from Corinth whom Paul mentions in his letters: he is a man who opened his home to Paul and the entire Church (Romans 16:23), thus demonstrating his hospitality and commitment to the brethren. Paul personally baptized him during his stay in Corinth, as he emotionally recalls in 1 Corinthians 1:14, emphasizing the rarity and significance of these baptisms he administered himself.
G1050I.origine: Gaius is a common Latin name in the ancient world, which literally means "he who rejoices." It was widely used in the Roman Empire, held by citizens, slaves, and associates. In the New Testament, several Christians bear this name, referring to different individuals depending on their city of origin.
G1050I.emploi: Gaius of Corinth is mentioned twice in Paul's epistles addressed to the churches. In 1 Corinthians 1:14, Paul remembers having baptized him personally, which shows his personal importance to the apostle and highlights the close link between baptism and the faith of the early Christians. In Romans 16:23, written from Corinth, Paul refers to him as "my host and that of the whole Church," revealing that he hosted the gatherings of believers in his home, likely because his house was large and welcoming enough. This detail illustrates the crucial role of private homes in the ecclesial life of early Christianity.
G1050I.portee: Gaius embodies the generosity and hospitality of the early Christian: he opens his home not only to an apostle but to the entire assembly of believers. His example teaches the reader that faith is concretely manifested through welcome, service, and sharing of resources. It is also a reminder that proper names in the Bible are not mere enumerations: they are real men and women whose faithfulness to Jesus has left a lasting mark.

sens: Christian from Macedonia
Christian from Derbe
Christian from Corinth
Recipient of the third epistle of John
G1050J.detail: 1. Gaius is a name borne by several Christians in the New Testament. The most notable for us is the Gaius of Corinth, with whom the apostle Paul stayed and who showed hospitality to Paul and the entire assembly (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14). 2. Another Gaius, from Macedonia, is mentioned in Acts 19:29 as a traveling companion of Paul. 3. A third Gaius, from Derbe, is cited in Acts 20:4 among the disciples who accompanied Paul. 4. Finally, a Gaius is the recipient of the third epistle of John, a short letter where John calls him "the beloved" and praises his hospitality towards itinerant brothers (3 John 1:1).
G1050J.origine: Gaius is a very common Latin name in Roman antiquity. It appears in Greek as Gaios and is frequently found in documents from the Mediterranean world. It was a simple and popular first name, held by men of all social conditions.
G1050J.emploi: Several Christians bore this name during the apostolic time. The Gaius of Corinth is particularly remarkable: Paul emphasizes that he welcomed the apostle himself and that his house was open to the entire local church, which shows his role as a generous leader in the Christian community. The Gaius addressed in 3 John is praised by the apostle John for his exemplary hospitality towards itinerant preachers, a vital virtue in the early Church. These different Gaiuses illustrate the apostolic concern to recognize faithful and welcoming brothers.
G1050J.portee: These men named Gaius embody hospitality and practical service towards the brethren, values that the apostles sought to cultivate and honor in the nascent Church. Their example reminds the reader that authentic faith is expressed through generous welcome and material help offered selflessly to those who work for the advancement of the Gospel.

sens: White nutritious substance produced by mammals to feed their young
Elementary teaching, simple, suitable for beginners
Basic spiritual food for Christians starting their faith journey
G1051.detail:
1. Milk is the white liquid produced by animals (cows, goats, sheep) to nourish their young. It is a natural and primary food. In 1 Corinthians 9:7, Paul mentions the worker who draws his sustenance from the flock he tends, particularly from the milk he obtains from it.

2. The Bible uses milk as an image of simplified teaching, accessible to children or beginners. In 1 Corinthians 3:2, Paul reproaches the Corinthians for being able to receive only "milk" — that is, elementary truths — and not "solid food," which represents deeper and more demanding teachings. They still lack maturity.

3. For young converts, milk refers to fundamental spiritual nourishment. In 1 Peter 2:2, the apostle invites believers to "desire like newborn infants the pure spiritual milk," meaning to eagerly seek the foundational principles of faith that will help them grow. In Hebrews 5:13, the one who "is on milk" is a child in faith, inexperienced in divine righteousness.
G1051.origine: The Greek word gala (γάλα) comes from a very ancient root denoting milk, which is found in several Indo-European languages. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is halav (חלב), which has the same literal and metaphorical meaning. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses gala to translate halav. The word has no special etymology: it simply names this vital substance known to all since childhood.
G1051.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, always in Greek as gala. Only once does it retain its concrete literal meaning: in 1 Corinthians 9:7, where Paul refers to the milk of the flock as the natural wage of the one who tends it. Everywhere else, and this is essential, milk is a figure of teaching suited for beginners. Paul uses it to reproach the Corinthians for their spiritual immaturity (1 Corinthians 3:2), while the epistle to the Hebrews employs it to stigmatize Christians who remain at the elementary stage instead of progressing towards deeper understanding (Hebrews 5:12, 5:13). In Peter's case, the "pure spiritual milk" becomes a positive image: it is the desirable food by which newborns in Christ grow (1 Peter 2:2). From a reproach to an exhortation, the word changes tone without leaving its metaphorical field.
G1051.portee: This image of milk speaks to the heart of every Christian. It reminds us that spiritual life has stages: we start simple and childlike before maturing. It invites us not to remain stuck in the rudiments but to progress towards a richer understanding of God and His Word (Hebrews 5:12-13). But it also indicates that the basic elements are never to be despised — it is good milk, spiritual and pure, which we rightly hunger for. It helps to discern between the carnal malice that refuses to grow and the legitimate hunger of the new believer who needs to be nourished.

sens: a person from Galatia, a region in Asia Minor
a member of the Christian church established in Galatia
G1052.detail: 1. A Galatian is an inhabitant of Galatia, a region in central Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey) originally populated by Celts from the Balkans. The term thus designates a person belonging to this people. 2. In the New Testament, the term applies to Christians converted in the churches of Galatia, whom Paul directly addresses: "O foolish Galatians!" (Galatians 3:1). These believers are the recipients of the letter to the Galatians, where Paul warns them against legalism.
G1052.origine: The Greek word comes from the Greek ethnonym for the Celts (Κέλται, Keltai). The Galatians are historically Celtic tribes that settled in Asia Minor around the 3rd century BC. Their name reflects this Celtic-Balkan origin. Galatia became a Roman province in the 1st century during Paul's ministry.
G1052.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the letter to the Galatians (3:1 and 6:18). In both cases, Paul addresses his Christian readers in Galatia. In Galatians 3:1, he calls them with some exasperation, rebuking them for yielding to a teaching that diverts them from faith in Christ alone. The context shows that Paul specifically targets the churches he founded or visited in Galatia, rather than the entire population.
G1052.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that the Gospel transcends ethnic and geographical boundaries: Paul teaches non-Jews in a distant region with as much passion as in Judea. It is a testimony to the life of the early churches scattered throughout the Roman Empire, where faith in Jesus unites believers from different peoples.

sens: Historical region of Asia Minor populated by Gauls in the 3rd century BC
Roman province encompassing this region at the time of the New Testament
G1053.detail: 1. Galatia is primarily a geographical region in north-central Asia Minor (now Turkey), colonized by Celtic peoples from Gaul; it retains this Celtic name for several centuries after their settlement (2 Timothy 4:10 mentions it as a travel destination). 2. In apostolic times, Galatia is a Roman province that extends beyond the historical Celtic region, encompassing larger territories in central Asia Minor (Galatians 1:2 refers to all the churches established there by Paul).
G1053.origine: The name "Galatia" comes from the Galatians, a Celtic people who migrated from Europe to Asia Minor in the 3rd century BC. These Gauls maintained their cultural identity and name even after settling in the East. The Romans, upon conquering the region, adopted this name to designate the administrative province they created beyond the historical Galatian borders.
G1053.emploi: Galatia appears four times in the New Testament, always as a region or province where Paul established churches: in 1 Corinthians 16:1 and Galatians 1:2, Paul addresses the churches in this region and calls them to contributions or solidarity; in 2 Timothy 4:10, it is mentioned as a travel location; in 1 Peter 1:1, it is listed among the regions where scattered believers live. These usages show that Galatia was a center of active Christian life and an important stop in the apostolic ministry.

sens: historical and geographical region in central Asia Minor
G1054.detail: 1. Galatia is a region in central Asia Minor (now in Turkey) inhabited by Galatians, a people of Celtic origin. Paul travels through or stays in this region during his missionary journeys: in Acts 16:6, the Holy Spirit prevents him from preaching the word in Asia, and he travels through Phrygia and Galatia; in Acts 18:23, after some time in Antioch, he again travels through Galatia and Phrygia to strengthen the disciples there.
G1054.origine: The name "Galatia" comes from the Greek "Galatikos," which designates what belongs to the Galatians. Galatians (Γαλάται) is the Greek name for the Gauls, a Celtic people who settled in Asia Minor around the 3rd century BC. The region bears the name of its inhabitants. The Apostle Paul addresses an entire letter to the churches of Galatia (the letter to the Galatians), showing the importance of this region for early Christians.
G1054.emploi: Galatia appears twice in Acts, in chapters 16 and 18, during Paul's missionary journeys. In Acts 16:6, the Holy Spirit prevents Paul and his companions from preaching the word in Asia, leading them to travel through Phrygia and Galatia to other destinations. In Acts 18:23, Paul visits Galatia and Phrygia again to strengthen the disciples of the established churches. These passages show that Galatia was an important mission field: Paul founded Christian communities there to which he later writes his letter to the Galatians to defend the freedom of faith against legalism.
G1054.portee: Galatia reminds the reader that the Gospel spread well beyond Jerusalem and Palestine, even into the most distant pagan regions. It also illustrates the role of the Holy Spirit in guiding the apostles: it is the Spirit who directs Paul where his mission is truly needed. Finally, this region is the birthplace of a foundational letter on grace and Christian freedom.

sens: absence of wind and agitation on the water
state of rest and serenity
restored inner peace
G1055.detail: 1. Calm is primarily the absence of wind and the stillness of the water: it is a concrete meteorological and maritime state. In Mark 4:39, Jesus calms a furious storm, and calm returns to the sea — the wind ceases, the waves settle, everything becomes peaceful. 2. By extension, calm denotes a general state of rest and serenity after trouble or fear. The disciples, terrified by the storm (Luke 8:24), regain calm with the wind and waves settling. 3. Calm can also evoke inner peace, the rest of the soul in the face of panic. Jesus asks the disciples why they are afraid when he is with them (Matthew 8:26) — he offers them not only external calm but also inner confidence.
G1055.origine: The Greek word galēnē comes from a root that evokes the absence of storm and the rest of the elements. It designates the opposite of fury, storm, agitation. It is a simple and concrete word, directly related to the observation of the sky and the sea.
G1055.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the account of the calming of the storm: Matthew 8:26, Mark 4:39, and Luke 8:24. The three evangelists report the same miracle in slightly different ways. In each case, after Jesus commands the wind and the sea, a great calm occurs — the wind ceases, the waves settle. It is always the immediate and visible result of Jesus' intervention. The word emphasizes the violent contrast: before, the terrifying storm; after, the absolute and sudden calm.
G1055.portee: This word reminds Christians that Jesus is sovereign over the elements and over all that disturbs our peace. The calmed storm is not just a demonstration of power; it invites the disciple to trust Jesus in the very midst of panic, knowing that he can bring calm to our lives. The calm that Jesus gives thus surpasses mere absence of storm: it is a supernatural peace based on his presence and authority.

sens: Region in the northern part of Palestine in the Holy Land
Main area of activity for Jesus at the beginning of his ministry
Zone where the disciples and the first witnesses of his resurrection lived
G1056G.detail:
1. Galilee is the northern region of Palestine during the time of the New Testament, inhabited by both Jewish and Gentile populations. It is a fertile and populated area, with notable centers such as the city of Nazareth and the Sea of Galilee. Jesus retreats there to escape danger in Judea (Matthew 2:22).

2. It is in Galilee that Jesus begins his public ministry and performs most of his miracles and teachings. After his baptism by John, he returns to this region, "filled with the power of the Spirit," and his fame spreads quickly there (Luke 4:14).

3. After his resurrection, Jesus promises his disciples that he will go ahead of them there (Matthew 26:32), and it is in Galilee that the women are invited to remember his words: "Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee" (Luke 24:6).
G1056G.origine: The Greek word comes from the Hebrew "ha-Galil," which literally means "the circle" or "the district" — a well-defined and identified region. This name reflects the geographical and administrative importance of this area in the geography of the Holy Land. It is the direct translation of the Hebrew term used to designate this northern Palestinian region.
G1056G.emploi: The word "Galilee" appears 56 times in the New Testament, primarily in the four Gospels. Matthew, Mark, and Luke constantly refer to it to locate Jesus' ministry: his healings, his teachings, the calling of his disciples. John also uses it to locate the miracles (John 4:54: "Jesus performed this second miracle when he came from Judea to Galilee"). Galilee also appears in resurrection accounts, where it is the place where the disciples are to meet the risen Jesus. After the Gospels, it is mentioned in Acts as the origin of the first Christian community.
G1056G.portee: Galilee reminds the believer that salvation and the power of God are not reserved for prestigious centers (Jerusalem, the Temple) but are manifested in a region of Galilee often despised ("Can anything good come out of Nazareth?"). It is also the meeting place between the risen Jesus and his disciples, symbolizing grace and the continuity of the divine plan. For the reader, Galilee embodies the call to follow Jesus in the everyday and the ordinary.

sens: mountainous region in the north of Palestine
freshwater lake at the center of Galilee
G1056H.detail:
1. Galilee is primarily the mountainous region in the north of Palestine, crossed by trade routes and inhabited by diverse populations. It is where Jesus grew up in Nazareth and called his first disciples, fishermen by the sea (Matthew 4:18; Mark 1:16).
2. The term also refers to the freshwater lake that occupies the heart of this region, called the "Sea of Galilee" in the Gospels (Matthew 15:29; John 6:1). This lake, rich in fish, was the economic and social center of the life of its inhabitants.
G1056H.origine: The Greek name "Galilee" comes from the Hebrew "Galil," which means "circle" or "district." This name originally described an administrative or geographical district. In biblical Hebrew, the same word designates a defined region, like a watchtower that "oversees" an area. The name has been attached to this northern region of the Promised Land since Old Testament times.
G1056H.emploi: The word "Galilee" appears five times in the Gospel according to the Segond, always to designate either the region or the lake at its center. The accounts of the calling of the disciples (Matthew 4:18; Mark 1:16) situate the action by the "Sea of Galilee" where fishermen Simon Peter and Andrew lived. John also mentions this lake as the "Sea of Galilee" (John 6:1), sometimes called the "Sea of Tiberias" after a nearby city. Matthew and Mark describe Jesus leaving or crossing this region (Matthew 15:29; Mark 7:31), showing his preaching itinerary throughout Palestine.
G1056H.portee: Galilee is not the political center of Judaism (Jerusalem is), but it is the cradle of Jesus' ministry and the stage for his first miracles and teachings. It reminds the reader that God chose a peripheral region and a simple people — fishermen — to accomplish his work. The constant presence of the lake in the narratives also evokes the concrete context of the daily life of the disciples and the importance of material details in the Gospels.

sens: Inhabitant or native of Galilee
Disciple or companion of Jesus of Nazareth
Person recognizable by their accent or regional origin
G1057.detail:
1. A Galilean is a person from Galilee, the northern region of Palestine. Jesus himself was a Galilean, originally from Nazareth, and that is why he is called "the Galilean" (Matthew 26:69; Luke 23:6).

2. The term also refers to the disciples and companions of Jesus, all Galileans: the apostles are recognized and addressed because they come from Galilee, like Peter, who is told, "You are a Galilean" after spending time with Jesus (Mark 14:70; Luke 22:59). At Pentecost, the crowd is astonished to hear the apostles speaking in various languages and asks, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?" (Acts 2:7).

3. The Galilean accent betrayed regional origin: it was an immediate sign of recognition that allowed someone to be identified, as seen when the servant girls recognize Peter by his speech (Luke 13:1, 13:2).
G1057.origine: The word comes from Galilee (Greek Galilaia, Hebrew Galil), which literally means "circle" or "region" — it is the circular region in the north of Palestine. The adjective "Galilean" naturally formed to designate the inhabitants of this region. In the Greek Old Testament, the same place is found under the name of Galilee, a land with often unstable borders and multiple influences.
G1057.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels and the early Acts. It mainly serves to identify Jesus and his disciples: Peter is recognized as "Galilean" (Matthew 26:69, Mark 14:70, Luke 22:59), Jesus is called "the Galilean" (Luke 23:6). The term can also refer to the inhabitants of Galilee in general, as in the account of the Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1, 13:2). Especially in Jerusalem, being a Galilean was a distinctive trait that marked the disciples: they were recognized by their accent (Acts 2:7). The word sometimes carries a nuance of contempt in the mouths of Judeans, who viewed Galileans as simple people, common folk.
G1057.portee: Being Galilean primarily means coming from a humble and peripheral region, far from the religious center of Jerusalem. Jesus, a Galilean, chose not to be a master of the Temple but an itinerant prophet sent to ordinary people. For the disciples, being recognized as Galileans reminds them that they had no official religious authority — they were neither priests nor scholars, just common men. This encourages the reader: God does not need prestigious figures to proclaim the Gospel. It is the power of the Holy Spirit, not origin or social status, that bears witness.

sens: Roman proconsul governing the province of Achaia
Magistrate before whom the Jews accused the apostle Paul
G1058.detail:
1. Gallio was the proconsul — that is, the Roman civil and military governor — of the province of Achaia, which included the city of Corinth. In Acts 18:12, he is presented as the Roman authority officially responsible for administering justice in the region.
2. When the Jews of Corinth accused Paul of violating the Mosaic Law, they dragged him before Gallio's tribunal, hoping he would punish him (Acts 18:12-14). However, Gallio refused to get involved in a Jewish religious dispute: he saw no violation of Roman law, and he dismissed the accusers (Acts 18:14). After that, a crowd beat Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, right in front of the tribunal, but Gallio did not care (Acts 18:17).
G1058.origine: This is the historical name of a Roman proconsul from the 1st century. According to ancient tradition, he was the brother of the philosopher Seneca. His Greek name Γαλλίων derives from the Latin Gallio.
G1058.emploi: Gallio appears only in three verses of chapter 18 of Acts, during Paul's stay in Corinth. He embodies Roman judgment in the face of the Jews' religious accusations: initially indifferent to theological disputes (Acts 18:14), he also becomes indifferent to the violence committed before his tribunal (Acts 18:17). His paradoxical inaction — both a refusal to judge a religious case and passivity in the face of aggression — shows that Roman authorities did not consider themselves competent to resolve internal disputes within the Jewish community.
G1058.portee: The episode of Gallio illustrates how, at the time of Paul's ministry, Roman authorities viewed Christian preaching as an internal matter of Judaism, not as a political threat. This relative neutrality allowed Christianity to develop without immediate legal persecution. For the believing reader, it shows how God providentially used the impartiality of human institutions to protect His nascent Church.

sens: 1st-century teacher of Jewish law
Teacher of the future apostle Paul
Influential Pharisee in the Sanhedrin
G1059.detail: Gamaliel is a master of the Torah, a recognized and respected rabbi among the Jews of Jerusalem during the time of the apostles. He appears in the Sanhedrin (the supreme judicial council) as a wise and moderate voice: when the apostles are brought to trial after Pentecost, it is he who, esteemed by all the people, asks that they be taken out before pleading not to condemn them too hastily (Acts 5:34). Later, Paul reveals that he was his student in Jerusalem and received rigorous training from him in the precise knowledge of the law of the fathers (Acts 22:3). The name itself means "God is my reward" in Hebrew.
G1059.origine: The name "Gamaliel" comes from Hebrew and literally means "God is my reward." It is borne by a well-known historical figure in Jewish tradition: Gamaliel the Elder, an extremely respected teacher of the law, probably from the early 1st century.
G1059.emploi: Gamaliel appears twice in the Acts of the Apostles. In Acts 5:34, he intervenes in the Sanhedrin to moderate the condemnation of the apostles who had just healed in the name of Jesus; his position as a teacher of the law and his prestige among the people give him considerable moral authority. In Acts 22:3, Paul mentions him as his own teacher, at whose feet he was raised and instructed: this shows the influence that this rabbi had on promising young Jews of the time, particularly on the one who would become the apostle to the Gentiles.
G1059.portee: Gamaliel embodies the figure of the just and wise teacher, capable of temperance even in the face of great religious conflicts. His intervention reminds the reader that there were thoughtful and prudent voices within 1st-century Judaism. It also shows that Paul, before his conversion, was not ignorant: he had received the best rabbinical training available, which makes his transformation in Damascus all the more radical and authentic.

sens: for the man: to take a woman, to contract marriage with her
for the woman: to enter into marriage, to accept a husband
for either: to be married or to participate in marriage
G1060.detail:
1. When a man marries, he "takes a woman" — this is the act by which he legally and publicly unites with her. In Matthew 5:32, the one who "marries a divorced woman commits adultery": the word refers to the act of forming the marital bond. It is the image of taking possession in the bond of marriage.

2. When a woman marries, she enters into marriage, yielding herself to a husband. In 1 Corinthians 7:39, the widow who wants to "marry" freely accepts a spouse. In women, the verb often emphasizes acceptance and entry into a new life.

3. The word is also used generally to say that two people are united in marriage, without emphasizing who acts: in 1 Corinthians 7:10, Paul commands "those who are married" to remain together. It is the state of marriage itself that is in view.
G1060.origine: The word comes from a root that denotes marital union. In the Greek of the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it primarily renders the Hebrew verb that means "to take" (in the sense of taking a woman as a wife). Marriage in the Bible is primarily conceived as a voluntary and legal act that unites two people before God.
G1060.emploi: The verb appears 25 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and in 1 Corinthians 7 (Paul's advice on marriage). It is used for the man alone ("the one who marries," Matthew 5:32), for the woman alone (Mark 10:12), or for both together. The word carries a moral weight when it concerns remarriage after divorce — Jesus speaks of it as adultery if the divorce is not justified. Paul also uses it to address the question: is it good to marry? (1 Corinthians 7). At the resurrection, marriage no longer exists (Matthew 22:30).
G1060.portee: This word reminds us that marriage is a concrete and sacred reality in God's view. Observing it in the places where Jesus speaks of it, we discover His intention: marriage unites a man and a woman in a lasting way, and it is only broken under certain conditions. For the believer, meditating on this verb invites us to see marriage not as an optional human arrangement, but as a covenant that God recognizes.

sens: To give a person in marriage, to betroth to a husband or wife
To enter into marriage oneself, to get married
To be united in marriage
G1061.detail:
1. The primary meaning is active: to give one's daughter (or a relative) in marriage, to arrange a marriage for her. This is the traditional role of the father or guardian, as seen when Jesus says that men "were marrying their children" before the flood (Luke 17:27) — that is, they were organizing marriages, controlling them, being the actors in them.
2. The verb also takes on a reflexive meaning: to marry oneself, to enter into marriage as a person. When it says "the wives of husbands" (Luke 20:35), it refers to the state of one who is married, who has taken a husband.
3. In Jesus' words about the resurrection, the word appears mostly in the passive to speak of a state: "they will neither take wives, nor will the wives of husbands" (Matthew 22:30). The resurrected will not be in the condition of marriage — they will not be "married."
4. The verb can also simply designate the man who is married, the husband (1 Corinthians 7:38), the one who has been "given" to a woman or who has bound himself to her in marriage.
G1061.origine: The word comes from γάμος (gamos), marriage, the conjugal union. Γάμος primarily denotes the act of marrying (the ceremony) and the state of marriage. The verb γαμίζω is regularly formed with the suffix -ίζω, which gives the noun an active sense: to perform the marriage, to marry someone. It is a common verb in everyday Greek.
G1061.emploi: The verb appears about 7 times in the Greek New Testament, mostly in the three synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and once in Paul. It always refers to marriage in a human or heavenly context. Jesus uses it twice in his teaching on the resurrection: to say that the resurrected will be "neither married nor given in marriage" (Matthew 22:30, Mark 12:25, Luke 20:35). He also recalls how people "were marrying and giving their children in marriage" in the days of Noah before the flood (Matthew 24:38, Luke 17:27). Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 7:38 to discuss the father's right to marry — or not — his daughter.
G1061.portee: This word raises a crucial question: is marriage eternal? Jesus asserts that in the world to come, at the resurrection, the righteous will neither be married nor given in marriage, but will be "like the angels." This is a call to relativize earthly ties and to turn the heart toward the eternal God. Marriage remains good and legitimate in this life — people "get married" naturally and it is normal — but it is not the ultimate purpose of our existence. This word frees believers from the idea that marriage gives absolute meaning to life.

sens: Marriage ceremony and accompanying celebration
Wedding meal or banquet
State or relationship of marriage
G1062.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the marriage ceremony itself, with all the solemnity and joy it entails. In the parable of the king and his son (Matthew 22:2), Jesus speaks of the "wedding" as the great event for which the king invites people. It is a festive, public moment where the community gathers.
2. Very often, "wedding" means the feast, the banquet that accompanies and celebrates the marriage. The text specifies: "Behold, I have prepared my feast; my oxen and fattened cattle are killed, all is ready, come to the wedding" (Matthew 22:4). At Cana (John 2:1-3), Jesus turns water into wine at the wedding, which shows that the banquet was the heart of the celebration: people ate and drank there. There was a "wedding hall" (Matthew 25:10) where the meal took place.
3. More rarely, the word denotes the state of marriage itself, the conjugal relationship. The epistle to the Hebrews reminds us that "marriage must be honored by all" (Hebrews 13:4), where "marriage" translates the same Greek word: it is the institution of marriage, not the festive event.
G1062.origine: The Greek word γάμος (gamos) comes from a root that expresses union. In Hebrew, the Greek Scriptures of the Old Testament translated the Hebrew מִשְׁתֶּה (mishté), which means banquet or feast, with this word. The Greek gamos first has a concrete value: marriage experienced as a public event and community feast, before designating the conjugal relationship itself.
G1062.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the parables of Matthew (the parable of the wedding guests, 22:2-12) and in the account of Cana (John 2:1-3). It regularly denotes the wedding celebration with its meals (Luke 14:8: "do not take the first place" at the wedding) and its ceremonial garments (Matthew 22:11). Revelation (19:7, 9) uses it for the "wedding of the Lamb," an eschatological image of the definitive union between Christ and the Church. In these usages, "wedding" retains its primary meaning: a festive and joyful event, a community gathering around marriage.
G1062.portee: The word "wedding" reminds us that marriage, in the Bible, is never a private act: it is a celebration, a public covenant, an event that involves the community and deserves to be celebrated with joy. The parables where Jesus speaks of weddings invite reflection on the nature of the Kingdom of God: a banquet to which all are called, a joyful covenant between God and His people. The image of the "wedding of the Lamb" in Revelation opens a perspective of hope on the final union between Christ and the Church.

sens: introduces the reason or cause of what has just been said
states an established fact that confirms or explains the previous assertion
introduces a question or exclamation that supports what precedes
links a consequence or conclusion to what is prior
G1063.detail:
1. The word "for" simply introduces the reason or cause: it answers the question "why?" When Jesus says, "the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45), the "for" shows that this is the true nature of the Son of Man. Similarly, when Paul states, "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes" (Romans 10:4), the "for" explains why this must be believed: because that is what Christ is.
2. Often, "for" simply states a fact that confirms or clarifies what has been stated: it is an explanation by truth. In Matthew 2:2, the wise men seek the king of the Jews "for" (that is: it is an established fact that) His birth heralds a change. The "for" can also support an assertion by justifying it with a principle that undergirds it (Matthew 7:2: you will be measured as you measure, "for" this is the law of judgment).
3. Sometimes, "for" introduces a question or exclamation to reinforce what precedes. In Matthew 9:5, Jesus asks: "Which is easier to say: Your sins are forgiven, or to say: Rise and walk?" — the "for" (absent in French but present in Greek) emphasizes the challenge or rhetorical force of the question.
4. Occasionally, "for" states a consequence or consolidates reasoning: it connects what follows to what precedes in a way that shows logical continuity or natural implication, as in Romans 7:1 where Paul explains a legal principle by saying "for you do not know...".
G1063.origine: The Greek word γάρ comes from a very ancient contraction: "γε" (an emphatic particle meaning "at least" or "indeed") + "ἄρα" (a particle expressing a conclusion or consequence). This fusion produces a word that retains the force of these two elements: it affirms something in truth while logically connecting it to what precedes. The word was fixed very early in the history of Greek and belongs to both classical style and that of the New Testament. It is one of the most frequent words in both ancient Greek and the New Testament: it is the logical cement of thought.
G1063.emploi: The word "for" (γάρ) is used over a thousand times in the New Testament, making it one of the most frequent conjunctions. It always functions as a particle that extends and justifies the previous statement: it never introduces a new idea, but rather the reason or explanation of what has just been said. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke, it is constantly found in the words of Jesus or in the narrative to explain an action or command (Matthew 1:21, 2:2, Mark 10:45, Luke 1:15). In Paul, "for" is very frequent when he lays out his theological reasoning: each "for" anchors an assertion in a deeper truth or in a logical consequence (Romans 10:4, 1 Corinthians 11:5). Sometimes "for also" (and in Greek "and for") reinforces the explanation by adding an additional confirmation to the reason (Mark 10:45). The word has never really changed in meaning: it remains a tool for logical connection and justification.
G1063.portee: Understanding the force of the biblical "for" helps the reader grasp the logical architecture of the Christian faith. Every time the Bible asserts a truth and follows it with a "for," it invites the reader to see how that truth is rooted in another. Thus, when Paul says that our light afflictions produce an eternal weight of glory, the "for" that follows asks the reader to connect this comfort to the divine promise: it is a call to believe that the given reason is true. Ignoring these little words is a loss: one misses the structure of divine revelation that progresses through logical chaining rather than isolated statements.

sens: The belly, the lower part of the body
The uterus, the organ where the child develops
To be pregnant, to carry a child in one's womb
One who eats a lot, who is dominated by gluttony
G1064.detail: 1. The belly is the cavity of the body that contains the organs of digestion. This is the literal and anatomical sense of the word. 2. The uterus is the female organ where the child forms and grows for nine months before birth. 3. To be pregnant means that a woman is carrying a developing child in her womb: "Mary, His mother, was betrothed to Joseph, and she was found with child of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:18). This state begins at conception and ends at childbirth. 4. Figuratively, the belly can also refer to a person who is dominated by their carnal appetites, particularly gluttony: the Apostle Paul calls some "slaves of their belly" (Titus 1:12), meaning people who live only to eat and for pleasures.
G1064.origine: The Greek word gastēr comes from a very ancient root meaning belly or stomach, common to several Indo-European languages. In Hebrew, it translates the word beten (בטן), which has the same literal meaning. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), gastēr also renders Hebrew expressions for "to be pregnant" or "to conceive." The word evokes the image of the body filling up, expanding, hence its use to denote both the belly of one who eats and that of one who gives birth.
G1064.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, almost always to denote the state of pregnancy. The four Gospels use it to announce or describe the conception and birth of Christ: the Angel Gabriel tells Mary, "you will conceive and bear a son" (Luke 1:31), and Matthew reports that "Mary, His mother, was betrothed to Joseph, and she was found with child of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:18). Jesus also predicts the misfortune of "women who are pregnant" at the time of persecutions and the end of times (Matthew 24:19, Mark 13:17, Luke 21:23). The word also appears in a saying about the pains that will come suddenly: "As labor pains come upon a pregnant woman" (1 Thessalonians 5:3). Only once, in Titus 1:12, is it used figuratively to refer to a glutton, someone dominated by their belly.
G1064.portee: This word reminds the believer of the mystery of the Incarnation: God chose to come into the world through the womb of a woman, Mary, submitting to the most humble human realities. It also evokes the pain and vulnerability of pregnant women, which gives weight to Jesus' words about their distress in times of tribulation. Figuratively, it warns against slavery to carnal appetites: to live dominated by one's belly is to live according to the flesh rather than according to the Spirit.

sens: at a minimum, in the least favorable hypothesis
what I say or refer to in particular
more, all the more
in any case, nonetheless
G1065.detail:
1. The word marks a restriction or a minimum: "at least on this day" means that, even if you have lost other opportunities, you have this one (Luke 19:42). It indicates that below this point, there is nothing.
2. Often attached to a word to highlight it, to distinguish it, to emphasize it: "Do you understand what you are reading?" where γε emphasizes the act of understanding itself (Acts 8:30).
3. With other small particles, it reinforces reasoning by saying "all the more": if this is true, then at least that is true as well; hence sometimes the translation "all the more" or "rather" (1 Corinthians 6:3: we will judge angels, therefore all the more the matters of this life).
4. Very often, it simply means "in any case, at least": a nuance that removes the strength of doubt or objection by affirming an undeniable minimum.
G1065.origine: It is a very old small particle in Greek, rare in the common language of the time when the Gospels and Epistles were written, but frequent in ancient classical Greek. It likely derives from a root that suggests the idea of "marking, distinguishing, showing." It is not always translated into French: sometimes it remains silent, as it plays a very light role, almost like an inflection of the voice.
G1065.emploi: The particle γε appears 27 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and in the Epistles of Paul. It is rarely found alone (Luke 11:8, 18:5, Romans 8:32), but much more often attached to other small particles: ἀλλὰ γε (but at least), εἰ γε (if at least), καὶ γε (and at least), κἂν γε, etc. Its usage varies: it can reinforce a single word to highlight it, or serve the logic of reasoning to say "all the more." In older translations, it is rendered as "at least," "at a minimum," "this," "all the more," or it is left aside.
G1065.portee: This small particle teaches us how the biblical language works with emphasis and persuasion: it highlights what really matters in the statement. For the reader, it invites them not to pass lightly over a word or statement, but to pay attention to it. It also reinforces the logic of faith: if God judges angels, all the more does He govern our daily lives.

sens: Israeli military leader during the time of the Judges
Man who defeated the Midianites through cunning and faith rather than strength
G1066.detail: 1. Gideon is a judge of Israel who led a reduced army to victory against the Midianites, enemies who oppressed the people. His name means "he who destroys" or "destroyer" in Hebrew. 2. What characterizes Gideon is his boldness to trust God despite his doubts and fears: he achieved a decisive victory not by the number of his soldiers, but through humanly improbable means (trumpets, jars, torches), showing that it is God who saves, not human strength.
G1066.origine: The Hebrew name Gideon (גִּדְעוֹן) literally means "he who destroys" or "destroyer," derived from a root that evokes the action of cutting or slicing. In Hebrew, this name reflects Gideon's warrior role in the history of Israel. The biblical text recounts his exploits in the Book of Judges, chapters 6 to 8, where he is presented as one of the great figures of faith in Israel.
G1066.emploi: Gideon is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:32, in the heart of the famous "faith chapter" where the apostle lists the men and women of the Old Testament who placed their trust in God. He appears alongside Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, and Samuel — all characters whose journeys illustrate how faith in God produces extraordinary acts. His appearance in this list of witnesses to faith emphasizes that it is not his personal strength that made him great, but his trust in God.
G1066.portee: Gideon invites Christians to discover that God does not need powerful and numerous means to accomplish His purposes: He often chooses improbable paths, humanly desperate situations, to show His power and prove that it comes from Him alone. The mention of Gideon in Hebrews 11 reminds us that true victory in the Christian life comes from faith, not from our resources or strengths.

sens: A valley to the west and south of Jerusalem
A place of idol worship and refuse
The eternal punishment of sinners after God's judgment
G1067.detail:
1. Gehenna is primarily a real valley located to the west and south of Jerusalem. It is the "valley of Hinnom" or "valley of the son of Hinnom," a geographical place known to the Israelites since the Old Testament.
2. During the monarchy, this valley was the site of idolatrous practices: sacrifices were offered to the god Moloch, notably by fire. King Josiah poured out blood there to defile it and stop these abominations, and it became a dump where the city's refuse and corpses were thrown.
3. In the New Testament, Jesus uses the name of this polluted valley as a symbol of divine judgment: it is "the Gehenna of fire," the place where God eternally punishes sinners who refuse repentance. Whoever causes the little ones to stumble "will be thrown into Gehenna" (Matthew 5:29-30), and Jesus warns that one should not fear those who kill the body but rather Him who can throw into Gehenna (Matthew 10:28).
G1067.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew "גֵּי הִנֹּם" or "גֵּי בֶן־הִנֹּם" (valley of Hinnom, valley of the son of Hinnom), transmitted through Aramaic. The historical geographical name was transformed by the prophets and sages of Israel into a powerful image of divine punishment: as this valley once saw monstrous sacrifices and became a filthy dump, it symbolizes the definitive rejection from the kingdom of God. The authors of the New Testament take up this image to speak of the final judgment.
G1067.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, exclusively in Matthew (7 times), Mark (3 times), Luke (1 time), and James (1 time). Jesus speaks of it mainly to warn against serious sin, particularly the scandal of the little ones: it is better to lose a member than to fall into Gehenna (Matthew 5:29-30, Mark 9:43-47). It also designates the fate of Jesus' adversaries who reject His message: the Pharisees who make proselytes "children of Gehenna" (Matthew 23:15), or those who receive the judgment of Gehenna (Matthew 23:33). It is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus speaks of eternal torment with clarity.
G1067.portee: Gehenna reminds Christians that sin has eternal consequences and that God's judgment is real. This is not a threat that Jesus lightly waves: He speaks of what awaits those who reject Him. For the believer, it is a call to take repentance seriously, to turn their heart toward God, and not to let sin distance them from salvation. Gehenna is also a warning that God takes justice seriously.

sens: Garden or orchard located at the foot of the Mount of Olives, near Jerusalem
G1068.detail: 1. Gethsemane is a place referred to as a "garden" in the Gospels (John 18:1), located at the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley facing Jerusalem. The name comes from Hebrew and literally means "oil press": it was probably an orchard planted with olive trees, where olives were pressed to extract oil. It is here that Jesus used to withdraw to pray with his disciples (Matthew 26:36; Mark 14:32).
G1068.origine: The name Gethsemane comes from the Hebrew גֵּת שְׁמָנִי (guet shemanim), composed of "guet" which means "press" and "shemanim" which means "oil". This name reflects the use of the place: it was an olive orchard where the fruits were pressed to produce oil, a common activity in the Holy Land. The name thus precisely describes the function of the place.
G1068.emploi: Gethsemane is mentioned only twice in the Synoptic Gospels: in Matthew (26:36) and Mark (14:32), during the account of the last night of Jesus before his passion. In both cases, Jesus leads his disciples there after the Last Supper, has them sit down, and then withdraws to pray alone. It is in this garden that Jesus faces his spiritual agony, praying three times for the cup to pass from him. John simply calls it a "garden" (John 18:1) without giving its name. Gethsemane is the scene where Jesus fully accepts the will of his Father and submits to the passion he is about to endure.
G1068.portee: Gethsemane is the place of Jesus' authentic humanity: it is where he weeps, prays in distress, and struggles against the fear of death. This garden shows us that Jesus did not go to the cross without suffering, but that he went through agony and accepted the Father's will. For the believer, Gethsemane teaches that true prayer is not devoid of emotion or difficulty, but consists of submitting to God even when the road is hard.

sens: one who lives nearby
one with whom we share daily life
one whom we naturally invite to important moments in life
G1069.detail:
1. The neighbor is primarily one who lives near you, in the same neighborhood or village. It is someone you encounter regularly, whom you know by sight. In John 9:8, the neighbors of the healed beggar immediately recognize who he is: they saw him every day.

2. The neighbor is also one with whom we share the proximity of life: we know each other, we know who we are, we exchange. This is a familiar person, not an intimate friend, but someone from your immediate environment. When the poor man loses his drachma in Luke 15:9, he first calls his neighbors to share his joy, meaning his neighbors and friends: the two categories go together.

3. Finally, the neighbor is one whom we invite to celebrations and joyful moments in life, alongside friends and family. In Luke 14:12, the Lord teaches that when we hold a banquet, we should not only invite the rich among our neighbors, who might return the favor.
G1069.origine: The word comes from the Greek gè (the earth), because the neighbor is literally one who lives on the land next to yours. It translates the Hebrew shakhén which has the same root: shakhèn also means "to dwell nearby". It is a simple and concrete word, designating the daily reality of living side by side.
G1069.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels of Luke and John. Luke uses it twice in the parables of chapter 15: the shepherd and the lost sheep calls his neighbors to rejoice (verse 6), and the woman who lost her coin calls her neighbors (verse 9). In both cases, the neighbor is a natural witness, a familiar presence with whom joy is shared. In Luke 14:12, the Lord speaks of the rich neighbors we invite to feasts, placing them alongside family and friends. In John 9:8, the neighbors of the healed beggar recognize him and wonder: they are people who saw him regularly. In all cases, the neighbor is someone from the close and familiar environment.
G1069.portee: This word reminds us that the people who surround us daily — our neighbors — are part of our life and responsibility. Jesus values the joy shared with the neighbor, and he teaches not to make unjust distinctions in our invitations: the neighbor is no less worthy than a rich friend. It is a call to recognize humanity and proximity in ordinary life.

sens: To express joy, gladness through laughter
To be in joy, to rejoice
To experience pleasure, amusement
G1070.detail: 1. Laughter in the literal sense: it is the expression of happiness and cheerfulness. In Luke 6:21, Jesus promises the afflicted that they will be "in joy" — the Greek word specifically denotes this state of laughter, of happy satisfaction that replaces tears. 2.
